deep_why: The core task is measuring how well different embedding models capture meaning in financial text. The underlying principle is that sound evaluation requires representative test cases across multiple realistic scenarios—if you only test retrieval, you miss classification failures, and vice versa. This principle holds because embedding quality has different facets depending on the task: the same model might rank financial documents well but fail at sentiment discrimination. By systematically covering retrieval, sentiment, and categorization tasks drawn from real Japanese financial data, the benchmark exposes where general-purpose embeddings fall short in domain-specific settings. This lets researchers build models that actually serve Japanese financial professionals rather than guessing from English benchmarks.

The challenge is ranking items fairly when they come from four fundamentally different categories—publications, datasets, variables, tools—using a single retrieval system. The underlying principle is that a relevance judgment must be grounded in the user's actual intent, not forced into a one-size-fits-all score. When you build evaluation from real user queries, you capture the true relevance signals: a researcher asking for 'climate data' genuinely expects both papers and datasets in results. By letting an AI system generate consistent topic descriptions and assess relevance against those descriptions, the work trades some manual annotation labor for systematic, repeatable judging across diverse item types. This framework reveals whether modern search can truly serve diverse information needs within one interface.

Event analysis requires understanding information at multiple levels—from recognizing individual facts within a document to inferring relationships and narratives across many documents. The underlying principle is that no single task reveals all capability gaps; you need a progression from atomic details to global coherence. The authors design four ordered tasks—detection, relation, structure, induction—because each builds on the previous: if a model cannot find events, it cannot reason about their connections. By auto-annotating source data via a self-correcting framework and running models through this progression, they expose exactly where reasoning breaks down. This layered diagnosis lets the community understand what must improve for reliable event understanding at scale.

Deep-research agents must navigate the web through multiple hops, each step depending on reasoning from the previous one; training them requires examples that show this stepwise thinking, not just final answers. The underlying principle is that an agent learns reasoning by imitating reasoning trajectories—if you show only 'question goes to answer,' the agent cannot learn how to decompose problems or backtrack when stuck. By collecting 9000 multi-hop questions with step-by-step reasoning chains from a strong agent, then training new agents to follow similar patterns under reinforcement learning, they create a self-improving flywheel. The verifiable answers ground each step, allowing the system to learn which reasoning paths actually lead to correct conclusions. This dataset lets practitioners train agents that think transparently and recover from errors rather than gambling on single searches.

Personalization in long-running assistant relationships requires extracting, storing, and using memory about the user; evaluating this capability demands measuring the entire cycle, not just one piece. The underlying principle is that a memory system is only as good as its weakest link—brilliant retrieval cannot save poor extraction, and vast storage cannot help if the model ignores retrieved facts. The benchmark defines four measurable tasks—extraction, updating, retrieval, utilization—because each represents a critical bottleneck where current models fail. By starting with real human-LLM conversations and human-verified ground-truth memories, the authors ensure they measure genuine personalization, not synthetic performance. This end-to-end lens reveals why even strong models struggle to tailor responses when the memory pipeline breaks.

E-commerce moderation requires detecting policy violations even when they are deliberately hidden through obfuscation—word splits, euphemisms, cropped images. The underlying principle is that rule understanding and intent inference are two separate capabilities that must both succeed; a model might know the rules but misread intent, or infer intent correctly but miss the rule. Evasive content defeats this by forcing both skills simultaneously: the system must decode the hidden meaning and recognize it violates a specific policy. By creating a multimodal benchmark with annotated text and images spanning six violation types, the authors establish a unified test where both reasoning and linguistic/visual comprehension are required. This prevents models from appearing to work when tested in isolation while actually failing in the real adversarial setting.

Historical weather archives contain qualitative accounts—narratives of societal experience—that meteorological data alone cannot capture; retrieving and interpreting them requires handling noisy text, archaic language, and matching user intent. The underlying principle is that retrieval and reasoning are coupled: you cannot extract societal resilience from documents you do not retrieve, and retrieving irrelevant historical segments wastes reasoning effort. The benchmark defines two tasks—retrieval from one million segments, then assessment and question-answering from what you found—because this pipeline mirrors real climate research. By testing against documents with OCR errors and dated phrasing, it exposes where dense search fails on unfamiliar vocabulary while LLMs struggle to extract structured insights. This combination reveals the true bottleneck in making historical narratives usable for climate science.

Training retrieval agents on search behavior requires grounding their reasoning in actual source documents—the agent must explain not just what it thinks but which passage led to that thought. The underlying principle is that traceable reasoning teaches the agent to seek evidence rather than speculate; if each step must point to a document, the agent learns that reasoning without retrieval is hollow. The AgentSim platform ensures wide exploration of documents and validates steps through multi-model agreement and human review on disagreements, focusing human effort where it matters most. By building a corpus of over 100,000 verified steps grounded in real documents, the authors create training data where reasoning and evidence are inseparable. This teaches agents to be verifiable—a critical requirement for trustworthy search systems.

User simulation for information retrieval experimentation is powerful but adoption is hindered when it requires substantial coding setup; researchers need to compose experiments visually while maintaining reproducibility. The underlying principle is that simulation value depends on usability—a theoretically perfect simulator that requires days of engineering setup will not be used. By providing a web-based visual workbench for building simulation pipelines, version control for custom components, and explicit provenance tracking through experiment bundles, the work lowers the barrier without sacrificing rigor. Researchers can now experiment with different simulated user behaviors and see how they rank systems, then share their exact pipeline for others to verify. This accessibility-plus-rigor combination accelerates research by reducing friction in a bottleneck that was never the simulation math itself.

User simulators serve two distinct purposes—behaving like real people and producing valid system rankings—yet existing evaluation conflates them. The underlying principle is that these goals can conflict: a simulator might match real behavior statistics perfectly yet rank systems incorrectly if it emphasizes behaviors orthogonal to system quality. The toolkit establishes this distinction measurably by testing both objectives separately and correlating them. The key finding—that the standard 'human-likeness classifier' test has near-zero correlation with ranking validity—proves the distinction matters in practice. By providing validated benchmarks and showing which metrics (click-depth distance, Frechet distance over session patterns) actually predict ranking accuracy, the work enables practitioners to optimize simulators for their actual need: not realism for its own sake, but reliable system comparison.

Using language models to generate evaluation labels scales test collection creation, but their effectiveness varies across languages; this study tests Arabic, where evaluation resources are scarce and needed most. The underlying principle is that if an LLM can reliably label relevance and those labels produce consistent system rankings, it solves a real resource problem—costly human annotation becomes optional. By generating 10,000 Arabic labels from three LLMs and checking agreement on binary judgments and system ordering, the authors verify this works for Arabic as it does for English. The caveats—false improvements when evaluating perfect systems, and limitations with manual systems—are honest; they show where LLM labeling remains risky. This evidence-based validation gives Arabic IR researchers confidence to adopt LLM labeling where it is safe, freeing human effort for languages where it is not yet validated.

Retrieval systems encode queries as small neural networks that score documents, but one fixed network size cannot balance speed and accuracy; this work shows you can build 'nested' networks of different sizes that share learned structure. The underlying principle is that smaller networks can inherit knowledge from larger ones if trained properly—the large network learns rich patterns, then the small network captures the essential parts. By extending the Hypencoder with this nested learning approach inspired by Matryoshka representations, the system achieves the same effectiveness with 7 times fewer active parameters in-domain. This cuts scoring latency by 1.6-3.4 times without sacrificing quality, making practical deployment feasible. The nested approach trades training complexity for runtime efficiency, a sound tradeoff for systems that search billions of documents.

Expert search supports two modes—name-based queries for known people and topic-based queries for exploring expertise areas—yet most systems treat them identically. The underlying principle is that user behavior reveals the true structure of search: if people consistently switch modes within sessions after successful clicks, that switch is strategic, not random. By analyzing half a million queries with a lexicon-based classifier, the work shows that mode-switching is success-driven—clicks often precede a shift from names to topics or vice versa. This pattern suggests users refine their search strategy based on what they found. Understanding these dynamics—that expert search is multimodal and dynamic—lets system designers build tools that support both modes seamlessly and adapt to shifting intent. This mirrors real expertise discovery, where names and topics are intertwined.

Online advertising bidding faces delayed feedback—conversions arrive late due to attribution windows and privacy policies—making traditional closed-loop control unstable. The underlying principle is that when feedback is delayed, you must reason forward from context rather than react to outcomes; an LLM analyzing campaign content and historical trends can forecast spend needs robustly even if today's outcome data is incomplete. By splitting the system into two layers—high-level planning via LLM-generated daily spend bounds and low-level real-time bid adjustments via model predictive control—the work creates a hybrid that exploits different strengths. The LLM sees the big picture; the control system tracks minute-by-minute without waiting for conversions to arrive. This separation achieves +1.8% conversion improvement and stability under sparse data, a gain impossible for systems wholly dependent on lagged feedback.

Generative retrieval assigns each item a semantic ID, then ranks by generating item sequences; when user interactions change, the IDs become outdated but rebuilding from scratch is expensive. The underlying principle is that you can realign old IDs to new ones without retraining the entire retriever if the mapping is stable—if you compute new IDs from recent behavior, then teach the existing model to map old vocabulary to new semantics, the model stays compatible. By proving this alignment updates work across three benchmarks while cutting retraining compute by 8-9 times, the authors make semantic ID systems practical as data drifts. This sidesteps the false choice between stale IDs and full retraining, enabling retrieval systems to adapt to changing behavior without the catastrophic cost of a complete rebuild.
